title: Zinc Translocation from Coastal Soil to Wheat as Mediated by Zinc Supply Levels and Soil Property
content: The association between soil property and zinc (Zn) availability, as well as how would soil property affect the Zn translocation from coastal soil to wheat grain was not well understood. Pot study and field trial were conducted to examine the effects of soil property, and Zn application on grain yield and grain Zn concentration in wheat grown under coastal soils. Soil available Zn concentration positively correlated with concentrations of total Zn, total P, Olsen-P, and ammonia-N in soil. Zn concentration in aboveground plant negatively correlated with soil pH and Olsen-P. Total Zn accumulation in aboveground plant positively correlated with soil DTPA-Zn concentration, Zn concentration in aboveground plant, aboveground biomass, and root weight. Soil Zn supply and plant growth had direct effects on Zn utilization in wheat, while soil property, soil nutrients, and soil available nutrients had indirect effects on Zn utilization in wheat by affecting soil Zn supply and/or plant growth, as revealed by PLS-PM model. Grain yield and grain Zn concentration were increased by Zn application under low soil salinity, while Zn application under higher soil salinity did not increase grain Zn concentration. Soil Zn application increased both grain yield and grain Zn concentration of 20 wheat genotypes, while foliar Zn application further increased average grain Zn concentration without increase of grain yield. Adjusting Zn supply tailored to suitable genotypes according to soil property is of promise to reach Zn biofortification target together with a satisfactory wheat grain yield under coastal saline soils.
